description: Defines the six core layers of the Operations Maturity System, the operational domains contained within each layer, and how each layer's maturity progresses across the five levels.

layers.name: Direction
layers.question: Where are we going?
layers.purpose: Translate strategic intent into clear operational direction.
weakSignals: Strategy exists as a slide deck, not as operating decisions.
Teams cannot explain how their work connects to a business outcome.
Priorities shift constantly with no visible tradeoff logic.
Different leaders describe the strategy differently.
strongSignals: Every team can trace its work back to a specific outcome.
Tradeoffs and constraints are explicit, not implied.
Priorities are stable enough to plan against, and change is communicated deliberately.
Risk appetite is stated, not discovered after something breaks.

domains.name: Business Outcomes
domains.question: What outcome is this work actually supposed to produce?
domains.whatItIs: The specific, measurable results the business exists to produce, distinct from the activities performed to reach them.
domains.whyItMatters: Without named outcomes, teams optimize activity instead of results and cannot tell productive work from busy work.

domains.name: Customer Promise
domains.question: What are we committing to deliver, and to whom?
domains.whatItIs: The explicit commitment an organization makes to its customers about what they will experience, on what terms.
domains.whyItMatters: Operations without a stated promise has no standard to design against, or to notice itself failing to meet.

domains.name: Objectives
domains.question: What are we trying to accomplish in this period, specifically?
domains.whatItIs: Time-bound, specific targets that translate strategy into something a team can actually plan against.
domains.whyItMatters: Vague objectives produce vague accountability; nobody can be behind or ahead of a target that was never defined.

domains.name: Constraints
domains.question: What limits are we actually operating inside?
domains.whatItIs: The budget, time, regulatory, technical, and capacity limits that bound what the organization can realistically pursue.
domains.whyItMatters: Plans built without naming constraints look ambitious on paper and fail on contact with reality.

domains.name: Risk Appetite
domains.question: How much risk are we willing to accept to move faster?
domains.whatItIs: An explicit statement of how much uncertainty, exposure, or potential loss the organization will tolerate in pursuit of its objectives.
domains.whyItMatters: Without a stated risk appetite, every risk decision is renegotiated from scratch, usually by whoever is most anxious in the room.

byLevel.likelyState: Strategy exists only as leadership intent; teams interpret direction independently and inconsistently.
byLevel.primaryRisk: Effort is spent on work that doesn't connect to any stated outcome, and nobody notices until results disappoint.
toReachNext: Write down the top three business outcomes for this period.
State the customer promise in one sentence.
Name at least one explicit constraint or tradeoff rule.

byLevel.likelyState: Direction is understood informally by tenured staff but isn't consistently communicated to newer team members.
byLevel.primaryRisk: Direction quality depends on who explains it, so alignment quietly degrades as the team grows.
toReachNext: Document objectives so they don't depend on verbal retelling.
Define priorities explicitly enough to resolve conflicts.
State risk appetite instead of deciding it case by case.

byLevel.likelyState: Objectives, priorities, and constraints are documented and generally consistent across teams.
byLevel.primaryRisk: Direction can go stale — teams keep executing last quarter's stated priorities even after circumstances changed.
toReachNext: Review and re-cascade direction on a fixed cadence.
Measure whether teams can trace their work to an outcome.
Track how tradeoff decisions are actually being made.

byLevel.likelyState: Direction is actively cascaded, tracked, and reinforced through a defined process.
byLevel.primaryRisk: Direction can become rigid, arriving as a mandate rather than an input teams can question with evidence.
toReachNext: Build feedback loops so execution evidence can inform strategy.
Formalize how risk appetite gets revisited as conditions change.
Track cascade speed from strategy change to team-level clarity.

byLevel.likelyState: Strategy and operating direction adjust deliberately as evidence, risk, and market conditions change.
byLevel.primaryRisk: Mature direction-setting can still outpace the organization's capacity to absorb change — verify Change Management keeps up.
toReachNext: Continue validating direction against leading indicators.
Formalize how frequently direction is deliberately revisited.
Extend cascade discipline to newly formed teams and functions.

layers.name: Design
layers.question: How should the organization work?
layers.purpose: Design the organizational architecture required to execute strategy.
weakSignals: The org chart describes reporting lines, not how work actually gets done.
Two teams both believe they own the same decision, or neither does.
Cross-functional work depends on personal relationships rather than defined interfaces.
Roles are titles, not accountabilities.
strongSignals: The operating model explains how capabilities combine to deliver outcomes.
Decision rights are explicit: who decides, who is consulted, who is informed.
Handoffs between functions are designed, not improvised.
Structure changes when the operating model changes, not the other way around.

domains.name: Organization Design
domains.question: Is the structure built around how work actually flows?
domains.whatItIs: The deliberate arrangement of teams, reporting lines, and groupings intended to support the operating model.
domains.whyItMatters: Structure that isn't derived from the operating model optimizes for reporting convenience instead of execution.

domains.name: Accountability
domains.question: Who answers for this outcome, regardless of who performed the work?
domains.whatItIs: The assignment of ownership for an outcome, as distinct from responsibility for performing a task.
domains.whyItMatters: Responsibility without accountability lets everyone point to their piece of the work while no one owns the result.

domains.name: Cross-Functional Interfaces
domains.question: How do two functions hand work to each other?
domains.whatItIs: The defined points where work, information, or decisions cross from one function or team to another.
domains.whyItMatters: Most operational failure happens at the seams between functions, not inside them.

domains.name: Service Models
domains.question: How does this function actually serve its internal or external customers?
domains.whatItIs: The definition of what a function provides, to whom, at what service level, and through what channel.
domains.whyItMatters: Functions without a service model negotiate their scope informally, request by request, forever.

byLevel.likelyState: Structure exists, but it reflects hiring history more than any deliberate operating model.
byLevel.primaryRisk: Work depends on informal relationships rather than designed interfaces, so it breaks when key people leave.
toReachNext: Name the organization's critical capabilities.
Identify where two teams believe they own the same thing.
Write down who currently makes which decisions.

byLevel.likelyState: Roles and ownership are recognized informally, but decision rights and interfaces aren't written down anywhere.
byLevel.primaryRisk: The same ambiguity gets resolved differently each time it comes up, depending on who's in the room.
toReachNext: Document decision rights for the most contested decisions.
Define at least one cross-functional interface explicitly.
Separate accountability from task responsibility in writing.

byLevel.likelyState: Operating model, roles, and decision rights are explicitly documented and mostly matched by behavior.
byLevel.primaryRisk: The design can fall out of date as the organization grows, while everyone keeps referring to the old chart.
toReachNext: Review the operating model on a fixed cadence, not just after a reorg.
Measure decision rights against how decisions are actually made.
Formalize cross-functional interfaces beyond the ones under active stress.

byLevel.likelyState: Design decisions are actively governed, and drift between design and actual behavior is caught quickly.
byLevel.primaryRisk: Governance overhead can start to slow the organization down if applied uniformly regardless of decision stakes.
toReachNext: Tier governance by decision risk and reversibility.
Track decision-rights conflicts as a monitored metric.
Build a standard process for redesigning around new capabilities.

byLevel.likelyState: Organization design evolves deliberately as strategy, scale, and capability needs shift.
byLevel.primaryRisk: Frequent redesign can itself become a source of instability if not paced against the organization's absorption capacity.
toReachNext: Sequence design changes against change-management capacity.
Continue validating that structure still matches how value flows.
Extend design discipline to newly acquired or merged teams.

layers.name: Execution
layers.question: How does work actually happen?
layers.purpose: Create repeatable systems through which work produces value.
weakSignals: Execution quality depends on who happens to be doing the work.
SOPs exist but nobody follows them, or nobody remembers they exist.
Handoffs lose information, context, or accountability.
Escalation is the default way problems get resolved.
strongSignals: Processes are documented, owned, and consistently followed.
Standards and controls catch problems before they reach the customer.
Automation removes manual toil from stable, well-understood processes.
Handoffs are explicit, with clear inputs, outputs, and owners.

domains.name: Workflow Design
domains.question: What is the actual sequence of steps this work follows?
domains.whatItIs: The deliberate design of task sequence, branching, and routing within a process.
domains.whyItMatters: Undesigned workflow accretes steps nobody remembers the reason for, and loses steps nobody assigned.

domains.name: SOPs
domains.question: Could someone new do this correctly using only what's written down?
domains.whatItIs: Written, step-by-step instructions for performing a specific task consistently.
domains.whyItMatters: SOPs are the artifact, not the maturity — see Process Ownership for what actually keeps them true.

domains.name: Standards
domains.question: What does 'done correctly' mean for this work?
domains.whatItIs: The explicit definition of acceptable quality, format, or method that execution is expected to meet.
domains.whyItMatters: Without stated standards, good work is whatever the reviewer personally prefers that day.

domains.name: SLAs
domains.question: How fast, and how reliably, are we committing to deliver this?
domains.whatItIs: A defined commitment on the speed and reliability of a service or process, usually with a measurable threshold.
domains.whyItMatters: Without an SLA, 'too slow' is a matter of opinion, and every delay is negotiated after the fact.

domains.name: Exception Management
domains.question: What happens when this case doesn't fit the standard process?
domains.whatItIs: The deliberate handling path for cases that fall outside a process's normal design.
domains.whyItMatters: Unmanaged exceptions either get forced through a process that wasn't built for them, or quietly become their own undocumented process.

domains.name: Escalation
domains.question: When should this move to someone else, and to whom?
domains.whatItIs: The defined path and threshold for moving a decision or problem to a different owner.
domains.whyItMatters: Escalation without defined thresholds becomes a habit rather than a mechanism — see Decision Rights for the deeper cause.

domains.name: Technology Enablement
domains.question: Does the system support how the work actually needs to happen?
domains.whatItIs: The alignment of tools and systems to the process they are meant to support, rather than the reverse.
domains.whyItMatters: Technology introduced before the process is understood usually digitizes the workaround, not the fix.

domains.name: Automation
domains.question: Is this task suitable to remove from human execution entirely?
domains.whatItIs: The replacement of a manual, well-understood, stable task with a system that performs it without human execution.
domains.whyItMatters: Automating an unstable or undocumented process just makes its failures faster and harder to trace.

byLevel.likelyState: Execution quality depends on who is doing the work; there is no shared, reliable method.
byLevel.primaryRisk: The organization is one departure away from losing the ability to perform a critical process at all.
toReachNext: Document the actual steps of your most critical process.
Name a single accountable owner for it.
Identify where the process most often breaks down.

byLevel.likelyState: Informal patterns exist and tenured staff can describe 'how we usually do it,' but execution still varies.
byLevel.primaryRisk: Quality and speed swing with individual judgment, and nobody can predict which version of the process will run.
toReachNext: Turn the informal pattern into a written standard.
Define what 'done correctly' means explicitly.
Give the process owner real authority to enforce the standard.

byLevel.likelyState: Standards, ownership, and documented processes exist and are generally followed.
byLevel.primaryRisk: Documentation can quietly diverge from practice once nobody is actively checking that the two still match.
toReachNext: Add controls that catch deviation before it reaches a customer.
Track handoff quality between teams, not just within them.
Build a defined path for handling exceptions.

byLevel.likelyState: Execution is actively controlled: deviations are caught, escalation paths work, and performance is measured.
byLevel.primaryRisk: Controls calibrated for yesterday's risk can create friction without adding protection as conditions change.
toReachNext: Review controls periodically against actual failure data.
Begin automating the most stable, well-controlled steps.
Measure handoff and exception rates as standing metrics.

byLevel.likelyState: Execution is resilient, measured, and improved continuously, with automation applied where it earns its cost.
byLevel.primaryRisk: Automation can outpace the organization's ability to safely change what's now running unattended.
toReachNext: Continue expanding automation only where it earns its cost.
Feed execution data back into process redesign, not just monitoring.
Extend the same rigor to newly added processes as they're created.

layers.name: Management
layers.question: How do we run the system every day?
layers.purpose: Create the mechanisms that actively manage execution.
layers.highlight: Processes don’t run organizations. Management systems run processes.
weakSignals: Meetings happen on schedule but no decisions come out of them.
Capacity is invisible until something is already late.
Issues are managed reactively, one fire at a time.
Change lands on teams with no plan for absorbing it.
strongSignals: Operating rhythms exist to make and track decisions, not just to meet.
Capacity and demand are visible and actively balanced.
Risks and issues are tracked to resolution, not just discussed.
Change is sequenced against the team's actual capacity to absorb it.

domains.name: Performance Management
domains.question: How do we know if a person or team is performing well?
domains.whatItIs: The mechanisms for setting performance expectations, observing actual performance, and responding to gaps.
domains.whyItMatters: Without a performance management system, feedback is sporadic, inconsistent, and disconnected from actual outcomes.

domains.name: Resource Planning
domains.question: Do we have the people and budget this plan actually requires?
domains.whatItIs: The deliberate matching of people, budget, and time to planned work before it is committed to.
domains.whyItMatters: Plans built without resource planning are aspirations, not commitments.

domains.name: Prioritization
domains.question: What gets worked on first when everything can't be done at once?
domains.whatItIs: The day-to-day sequencing of work within a team, distinct from strategic prioritization at the organizational level.
domains.whyItMatters: Without an explicit sequencing method, prioritization defaults to whoever asked most recently or most loudly.

domains.name: Issue Management
domains.question: Where do problems go once someone notices them?
domains.whatItIs: The system for capturing, tracking, and resolving operational problems to closure.
domains.whyItMatters: Without issue management, problems are solved once, informally, and resurface with no memory that they happened before.

domains.name: Risk Management
domains.question: What could go wrong here, and who is watching for it?
domains.whatItIs: The ongoing practice of identifying, tracking, and mitigating operational risk before it becomes an incident.
domains.whyItMatters: Risk that isn't tracked is discovered instead of managed — usually at the worst possible time.

domains.name: Change Management
domains.question: How is this change being sequenced against everything else in flight?
domains.whatItIs: The deliberate planning of how a change is introduced, communicated, and absorbed by the people affected by it.
domains.whyItMatters: Change introduced without a management plan competes with existing work for the same finite attention and capacity.

domains.name: Communication Architecture
domains.question: How does information reliably reach the people who need it?
domains.whatItIs: The deliberate design of what information flows where, through which channel, and on what cadence.
domains.whyItMatters: Without a designed architecture, communication happens by proximity — whoever is in the room hears it, and everyone else finds out late.

byLevel.likelyState: There is no active management system; execution runs on individual effort and improvisation.
byLevel.primaryRisk: Problems are found by customers, not by any internal mechanism designed to catch them first.
toReachNext: Establish one recurring rhythm with a real decision to make.
Make capacity visible, even informally.
Create a single place issues get tracked instead of just discussed.

byLevel.likelyState: Management practices exist but vary by leader or team.
byLevel.primaryRisk: Execution depends too heavily on individual management behavior.
toReachNext: Establish operating rhythms.
Establish performance standards.
Establish escalation mechanisms.
Establish capacity visibility.

byLevel.likelyState: Operating rhythms, capacity tracking, and issue management are defined and consistently used.
byLevel.primaryRisk: The mechanisms exist but may not yet be tested under real pressure — verify they hold up during a crunch, not just in steady state.
toReachNext: Track whether rhythms actually produce decisions, not just discussion.
Use capacity data to make prioritization tradeoffs, not just report status.
Add a defined process for managing change alongside existing work.

byLevel.likelyState: Management systems are actively governed: decisions are tracked to completion and capacity drives real tradeoffs.
byLevel.primaryRisk: A well-managed system can still fail to adapt if it isn't allowed to evolve — process can calcify into ritual.
toReachNext: Periodically review whether each rhythm still earns its place.
Forecast capacity, not just track current utilization.
Formalize how competing changes get sequenced against each other.

byLevel.likelyState: Management systems evolve deliberately, with rhythms, capacity models, and change practices refined based on evidence.
byLevel.primaryRisk: Sophistication can create a barrier to entry for new managers who haven't internalized why each mechanism exists.
toReachNext: Document the reasoning behind each rhythm so it survives leadership turnover.
Continue forecasting and stress-testing capacity models.
Extend management discipline consistently as the organization keeps growing.

layers.name: Intelligence
layers.question: How do we know what's happening?
layers.purpose: Turn operational activity into reliable information and decisions.
weakSignals: Dashboards exist but nobody changes a decision based on them.
Metrics are lagging only, so problems are visible after they've already hurt customers.
Different teams report different numbers for the same thing.
Data quality issues are common knowledge but never fixed.
strongSignals: Every core metric connects to a decision someone actually makes.
Leading indicators surface problems before they become customer-facing.
Metrics are trusted enough that people argue about the response, not the number.
Operational health is monitored continuously, not reconstructed after a failure.

domains.name: Leading Indicators
domains.question: What tells us a problem is coming before it arrives?
domains.whatItIs: Metrics that predict future performance rather than report on what has already happened.
domains.whyItMatters: An organization with only lagging indicators finds out about problems from its customers.

domains.name: Lagging Indicators
domains.question: What did we actually deliver?
domains.whatItIs: Metrics that report on outcomes after the fact, confirming what already happened.
domains.whyItMatters: Lagging indicators are necessary for accountability, but they arrive too late to change the outcome they describe.

domains.name: Quality Measurement
domains.question: How do we know the work meets the standard, not just that it got done?
domains.whatItIs: The measurement of whether output meets defined standards, as distinct from whether output was produced at all.
domains.whyItMatters: Volume metrics without quality metrics reward throughput even when throughput is producing defects.

domains.name: Dashboards
domains.question: Does this view actually change what someone does next?
domains.whatItIs: A visual presentation of metrics intended to support faster or better decisions.
domains.whyItMatters: A dashboard nobody acts on is reporting theater, not intelligence — see Operational Health for the discipline this requires.

domains.name: Forecasting
domains.question: What do we expect to happen, and how confident are we?
domains.whatItIs: The disciplined projection of future demand, performance, or risk based on current signals and trends.
domains.whyItMatters: Without forecasting, planning is always a reaction to what already happened rather than a preparation for what's coming.

domains.name: Customer Signals
domains.question: What is the customer experience actually telling us?
domains.whatItIs: Direct and indirect signals from customers — complaints, churn, satisfaction, behavior — read as operational input.
domains.whyItMatters: Customer signals often reveal operating system failures long before they surface in internal metrics.

domains.name: Employee Signals
domains.question: What is the workforce experience telling us about the system?
domains.whatItIs: Signals such as turnover, engagement, and workload strain, read as evidence of how the operating system is functioning.
domains.whyItMatters: Employee strain is frequently the earliest visible symptom of a capacity or process failure.

domains.name: Financial Signals
domains.question: What is the P&L or unit economics telling us operationally?
domains.whatItIs: Financial data read for what it reveals about operational performance, not just accounting results.
domains.whyItMatters: Cost and margin trends often surface an operational constraint well before it's visible in any operational metric.

domains.name: Decision Intelligence
domains.question: Does this information actually change a decision?
domains.whatItIs: The deliberate design of what information a decision-maker needs, in what form, at what moment.
domains.whyItMatters: More data does not create better decisions; the right data, connected to the right decision, does.

byLevel.likelyState: Metrics, where they exist, are reviewed occasionally but rarely change a decision.
byLevel.primaryRisk: Leadership finds out about serious problems from a customer or a public failure, not from an internal signal.
toReachNext: Pick the three to five metrics that matter most and define them once.
Assign an owner to each metric's accuracy.
Connect at least one metric to a specific recurring decision.

byLevel.likelyState: Some metrics are reviewed regularly, but different teams report different numbers for the same thing.
byLevel.primaryRisk: Meetings get spent debating whose number is correct instead of deciding what to do about it.
toReachNext: Establish a single source of truth for each core metric.
Document how each metric is calculated.
Retire metrics nobody is using to decide anything.

byLevel.likelyState: Core metrics are reliable, tied to specific decisions, and reviewed on a defined schedule.
byLevel.primaryRisk: Measurement may still be mostly lagging, so problems are confirmed after they've already affected customers.
toReachNext: Add leading indicators for your highest-risk processes.
Build a composite operational health view, not just individual metrics.
Actively monitor and fix known data quality issues.

byLevel.likelyState: Leading indicators catch problems early, and data quality is actively monitored, not just assumed.
byLevel.primaryRisk: A mature measurement system can still miss what it was never designed to look for, as the business changes.
toReachNext: Periodically ask what isn't currently being measured that should be.
Refine the metric set as the business model evolves.
Extend measurement rigor into newly formed teams and processes.

byLevel.likelyState: The measurement system itself is treated as a product: refined, pruned, and improved based on what's proven useful.
byLevel.primaryRisk: A highly tuned measurement system can create false confidence if its assumptions quietly stop matching reality.
toReachNext: Periodically re-validate that leading indicators still predict what they used to.
Continue pruning metrics that have stopped driving decisions.
Keep data quality monitoring itself under active measurement.

layers.name: Evolution
layers.question: How does the organization become better?
layers.purpose: Create an operating system capable of learning and adapting.
weakSignals: The same problems recur because only symptoms get treated.
Improvement happens in bursts, driven by whoever is frustrated this quarter.
Lessons learned are not captured, so mistakes repeat across teams.
New tools and automation get layered onto broken processes.
strongSignals: Root cause analysis is routine, not reserved for major incidents.
Improvement is continuous, measured against an established baseline.
Knowledge is captured and reused, not trapped in individual heads.
The organization treats its operating system as something it deliberately evolves.

domains.name: Experimentation
domains.question: How do we test a change before committing to it fully?
domains.whatItIs: The disciplined practice of testing a change on a limited scale before full rollout.
domains.whyItMatters: Without experimentation, every change is a full bet, and failure is expensive and hard to attribute.

domains.name: Innovation
domains.question: Where are we deliberately creating space for new approaches?
domains.whatItIs: The deliberate pursuit of new capabilities, offerings, or methods, distinct from optimizing what already exists.
domains.whyItMatters: An operating system tuned only for efficiency will optimize itself out of the ability to change direction.

domains.name: Process Optimization
domains.question: Is this process still the best way to produce this outcome?
domains.whatItIs: The ongoing refinement of an existing, stable process to improve its speed, cost, or quality.
domains.whyItMatters: Optimization applied to an unstable process locks in inconsistency instead of removing it.

domains.name: Automation Readiness
domains.question: Is this process stable and well-understood enough to automate?
domains.whatItIs: An assessment of whether a process has the standardization and stability required before automation is applied.
domains.whyItMatters: Automating a process before it's ready hard-codes today's inconsistency into tomorrow's system.

domains.name: AI Enablement
domains.question: Where would judgment or pattern-recognition at scale actually help this system?
domains.whatItIs: The deliberate identification of where AI-based tools can support decisions, execution, or analysis within a mature process.
domains.whyItMatters: AI applied to an undefined process automates ambiguity instead of resolving it.

domains.name: Knowledge Management
domains.question: Where does what we've learned actually live?
domains.whatItIs: The systematic capture, organization, and reuse of operational knowledge and lessons learned.
domains.whyItMatters: Without knowledge management, expertise leaves the building every time an experienced person does.

domains.name: Scaling
domains.question: What happens to this system at twice the current volume?
domains.whatItIs: The deliberate preparation of a process, team, or system to handle significantly more volume without proportional degradation.
domains.whyItMatters: Scale does not create operational ambiguity — it exposes ambiguity that was already there.

domains.name: Organizational Learning
domains.question: Does the organization get better at getting better?
domains.whatItIs: The organization's capacity to systematically turn experience into improved future performance, not just individual learning.
domains.whyItMatters: Without organizational learning, every team relearns the same lessons independently, at full cost, every time.

domains.name: Process Governance
domains.question: What keeps this process from drifting after it's been designed?
domains.whatItIs: The ongoing mechanism that reviews, approves, and controls changes to a process after it has been defined.
domains.whyItMatters: A process without governance decays the moment attention moves elsewhere.

domains.name: Maturity Management
domains.question: Are we deliberately advancing our own operating maturity, or just reacting?
domains.whatItIs: The active practice of assessing, targeting, and advancing the organization's operating maturity over time.
domains.whyItMatters: Maturity that isn't managed deliberately drifts backward under pressure, even after real progress has been made.

byLevel.likelyState: The same problems recur because only symptoms get addressed, one incident at a time.
byLevel.primaryRisk: The organization pays the cost of the same failure repeatedly without ever reducing its likelihood.
toReachNext: Run a real root cause investigation on your most recurring problem.
Write down what was learned somewhere others can find it.
Pick one baseline metric before attempting any fix.

byLevel.likelyState: Improvement happens in bursts, usually triggered by frustration rather than a deliberate process.
byLevel.primaryRisk: Gains from past improvement efforts erode quietly because nothing was standardized to hold them in place.
toReachNext: Standardize the last improvement that actually worked.
Set a baseline before starting the next improvement effort.
Create one place lessons learned get captured.

byLevel.likelyState: Root cause analysis and improvement work follow a defined process with a measured baseline.
byLevel.primaryRisk: Improvement can become procedural without becoming systemic — fixing instances instead of the conditions that produce them.
toReachNext: Track whether standardized fixes are actually holding over time.
Connect improvement priorities to your weakest measured layer.
Build a lightweight way to test changes before full rollout.

byLevel.likelyState: Improvement is measured against baselines, with clear decisions to standardize or roll back each change.
byLevel.primaryRisk: A well-managed improvement process can still stay reactive if it only responds to problems rather than anticipating them.
toReachNext: Begin experimenting proactively, not just in response to problems.
Assess which stable processes are genuinely ready for automation.
Formalize how lessons learned get applied across teams, not just within one.

byLevel.likelyState: The organization treats its own operating maturity as something to deliberately manage and advance.
byLevel.primaryRisk: Adaptive systems can still stagnate if the organization stops questioning its own assumptions.
toReachNext: Keep experimentation deliberate and evidence-based, not just constant.
Continue reassessing maturity targets as scale and strategy shift.
Extend organizational learning practices to every new team as it forms.
